terms.grammar: verb, second conjugation, with a dative of the person; accusative and infinitive for “convince that”, ut or nē + subjunctive for “persuade to”
evidence: Cic. Att. 1.5.8: tibi persuādeās tē ā mē frāternē amārī
Sen. Ep. 108.22: nec difficulter mihi ut inciperem melius cēnāre persuāsit
terms.comment: The person convinced is in the dative, so the passive is impersonal: mihi persuāsum est, I am convinced; mihi persuādērī numquam potuit, I could never be convinced (Cic. Sen. 80). Tibi persuādeās, “be sure”, closes Cicero’s letters to his family.

terms.gloss: I am convinced, I hold it as settled
terms.grammar: phrase; with an accusative and infinitive, often with sibi
evidence: Caes. B.G. 3.2: sibi persuāsum habēbant (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: A settled conviction, as in Caesar; for the moment of being won over, mihi persuāsum est.

terms.grammar: phrase; often with an accusative and infinitive
evidence: Cic. Brut. 187: fidem facit ōrātiō (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Of what wins belief, a speech or an argument; the person is in the dative.
Not “convince”: classically to convict of a crime or an error, or to prove a thing beyond doubt (Lewis & Short; see prove).

phrases.latin: cūrā ut valeās et nōs amēs et tibi persuādeās tē ā mē frāternē amārī
phrases.english: look after yourself, love us, and be sure that I love you as a brother

phrases.latin: cūrā ut valeās et ita tibi persuādeās, mihi tē cārius nihil esse nec umquam fuisse
phrases.english: take care of yourself, and be sure that nothing is dearer to me than you, or ever was

phrases.latin: patre itaque meō rogante … ad prīstinam cōnsuētūdinem rediī; nec difficulter mihi ut inciperem melius cēnāre persuāsit
phrases.english: so at my father’s request … I went back to my old habit; he had no trouble persuading me to start dining better

phrases.latin: Plēnus (-a) persuāsiōnis sum (+ acc. and inf.)

sources: Lewis & Short: persuadeo · Lewis & Short: fides · Lewis & Short: convinco
